claim: HCN channels control spontaneous electrical activity in heart and brain.
source: Hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated (HCN) channels control spontaneous electrical activity in heart and brain.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general property of HCN channels, supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: Binding of cAMP to the CNBD facilitates channel opening by relieving a tonic inhibition exerted by the CNBD.
source: Binding of cAMP to the cyclic nucleotide-binding domain (CNBD) facilitates channel opening by relieving a tonic inhibition exerted by the CNBD.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The structural mechanism coupling ligand binding to channel gating in HCN1 is unknown despite high resolution structures.
source: Despite high resolution structures of the HCN1 channel in the cAMP bound and unbound states, the structural mechanism coupling ligand binding to channel gating is unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: The HCN domain mechanically couples the CNBD and channel voltage sensing domain.
source: Here we show that the recently identified helical HCN-domain (HCND) mechanically couples the CNBD and channel voltage sensing domain (VSD), possibly acting as a sliding crank that converts the planar rotational movement of the CNBD into a rotational upward displacement of the VSD.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by computational and experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The HCND acts as a sliding crank that converts the planar rotational movement of the CNBD into a rotational upward displacement of the VSD.
source: Here we show that the recently identified helical HCN-domain (HCND) mechanically couples the CNBD and channel voltage sensing domain (VSD), possibly acting as a sliding crank that converts the planar rotational movement of the CNBD into a rotational upward displacement of the VSD.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model proposed based on computational and experimental data.

claim: Disruption of critical contacts between the VSD, HCND, and C-linker affects cAMP- and voltage-dependent gating in three HCN isoforms.
source: This mode of operation and its impact on channel gating are confirmed by computational and experimental data showing that disruption of critical contacts between the three domains affects cAMP- and voltage-dependent gating in three HCN isoforms.
evidence: This is supported by the mutagenesis experiments presented in the Results section.

claim: HCN channels are the molecular determinants of the If/Ih current.
source: Hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated (HCN) channels (Gauss et al., 1998; Ludwig et al., 1998; Santoro et al., 1997; Santoro et al., 1998) are the molecular determinants of the If/Ih current, a mixed Na+/K+ current that controls pacemaking in cardiac and neuronal cells (DiFrancesco, 1993; Pape, 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: The If/Ih current is a mixed Na+/K+ current that controls pacemaking in cardiac and neuronal cells.
source: Hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated (HCN) channels (Gauss et al., 1998; Ludwig et al., 1998; Santoro et al., 1997; Santoro et al., 1998) are the molecular determinants of the If/Ih current, a mixed Na+/K+ current that controls pacemaking in cardiac and neuronal cells (DiFrancesco, 1993; Pape, 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations.

claim: HCN channels are activated by hyperpolarization of membrane voltage.
source: Unique among voltage-gated channels, HCN channels are activated by hyperpolarization of membrane voltage.
evidence: This is a well-established property of HCN channels stated in the Introduction.

claim: Upon activation, HCN channels' inwardly directed cation current slowly depolarizes pacemaker cells to the threshold for action potential firing.
source: Upon activation, their inwardly directed cation current slowly depolarizes pacemaker cells to the threshold for action potential firing.
evidence: This describes the functional role of HCN channels in pacemaking.

claim: cAMP enhances HCN channel open probability, shifting the voltage-dependency of opening to more positive values and increasing the amount of current at any given voltage.
source: In addition to voltage, HCN channels are modulated by the second messenger cAMP, which enhances channel open probability, thus shifting the voltage-dependency of opening to more positive values and increasing the amount of current at any given voltage (Wainger et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: In the sinoatrial node, cAMP regulation of native HCN channels underlies the autonomic regulation of the heartbeat.
source: Regulation by cAMP of native HCN channels plays crucial physiological roles: in the sinoatrial node, it underlies the autonomic regulation of the heartbeat (DiFrancesco and Tortora, 1991);
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: In peripheral neuropathic pain, cAMP modulation of HCN channels leads to neuronal hyperexcitability enhancing pain transmission.
source: in pathophysiological conditions, such as in peripheral neuropathic pain, cAMP modulation of HCN channels leads to neuronal hyperexcitability enhancing pain transmission (Emery et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: The structure of HCN1 was recently solved.
source: The recently solved structure of HCN1 (Lee and MacKinnon, 2017) substantially advanced our comprehension of HCN channel architecture.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Each subunit of the tetrameric HCN channel is formed by six (S1-S6) transmembrane domains.
source: Each subunit of the tetrameric channel is formed by six (S1-S6) transmembrane domains (TM).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction based on the HCN1 structure.

claim: Helices S1-S4 form the voltage sensor domain (VSD) in HCN channels.
source: Helices S1-S4 form the voltage sensor domain (VSD), which is connected to the pore domain (helices S5-S6).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction based on the HCN1 structure.

claim: The C terminal cytosolic domain of HCN channels includes the C-linker and the cyclic nucleotide-binding domain (CNBD).
source: The C terminal cytosolic domain, attached to the end of TM S6, includes the C-linker (helices A' and B' connected via a loop to helices C' and D') and the cyclic nucleotide-binding domain (CNBD), a beta strand-alpha helix fold that hosts the cAMP binding pocket (Zagotta et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: The HCN1 structure revealed that a conserved sequence at the cytosolic N terminus, named HCN domain (HCND), folds into three short helices that wedge in between the VSD and C-linker.
source: The HCN1 structure further revealed that a conserved sequence at the cytosolic N terminus, named HCN domain (HCND), folds into three short helices (HCNa, HCNb and HCNc) that wedge in between the VSD and C-linker (Lee and MacKinnon, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: The tetrameric HCN1 channel shows a modular architecture with the two regulatory domains, the VSD and the C-linker/CNBD, connected to either side of the pore and seemingly bridged by the HCN domain.
source: Thus, the tetrameric HCN1 channel shows a modular architecture with the two regulatory domains, the VSD and the C-linker/CNBD, respectively, connected to either side of the pore and seemingly bridged by the HCN domain.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction based on the HCN1 structure.

claim: The membrane-embedded VSD is connected to the N terminus of the pore via the S4-S5 linker.
source: The membrane-embedded VSD is connected to the N terminus of the pore via the S4-S5 linker.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as a structural feature.

claim: The VSD moves within the electrical field upon hyperpolarization.
source: The VSD moves within the electrical field upon hyperpolarization (Bell et al., 2004; Männikkö et al., 2002; Vemana et al., 2004) but it is not yet clear how this movement is coupled to pore opening.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations.

claim: It is not yet clear how the VSD movement is coupled to pore opening in HCN channels.
source: The VSD moves within the electrical field upon hyperpolarization (Bell et al., 2004; Männikkö et al., 2002; Vemana et al., 2004) but it is not yet clear how this movement is coupled to pore opening.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as a knowledge gap.

claim: In the closely related SpHCN channel, the S4-S5 linker can be cut without compromising voltage gating.
source: Indeed, in the closely related SpHCN channel, the S4-S5 linker can be cut without compromising voltage gating (Flynn and Zagotta, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of HCN1 reveals a parallel arrangement of TM S4 and S5, comprising multiple contacts between these domains, which may serve to directly transmit the VSD movement to the pore without the need for an involvement of the S4-S5 linker.
source: A potential mechanism of coupling between the VSD and the pore has been proposed based on the cryo-EM structure of HCN1 (Lee and MacKinnon, 2017). This structure reveals a parallel arrangement of TM S4 and S5, comprising multiple contacts between these domains, which may serve to directly transmit the VSD movement to the pore without the need for an involvement of the S4-S5 linker (Cowgill et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations.

claim: The four C-linkers tetramerize to form a disc-like structure, called the 'gating ring'.
source: The four C-linkers are a continuation of the S6 pore helices and tetramerize to form a disc-like structure, called the 'gating ring'.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as a structural feature.

claim: Binding of cAMP to the CNBD induces an iris-like rotation in the gating ring, which is thought to help unwrap the bundle of S6 helices and open the pore.
source: Binding of cAMP to the CNBD induces an iris-like rotation in the gating ring, which is thought to help unwrap the bundle of S6 helices and open the pore (Gross et al., 2018; Lee and MacKinnon, 2017; Marchesi et al., 2018; Shin et al., 2004; Weißgraeber et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Voltage is both necessary and sufficient to open HCN channels.
source: Voltage is both necessary and sufficient to open the channel, as HCN1 mutants lacking the cytosolic C-linker/CNBD domain are fully regulated by voltage (Wainger et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: HCN1 mutants lacking the cytosolic C-linker/CNBD domain are fully regulated by voltage.
source: Voltage is both necessary and sufficient to open the channel, as HCN1 mutants lacking the cytosolic C-linker/CNBD domain are fully regulated by voltage (Wainger et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: The VSD does not require the rotation of the C-linker gating ring in order to open the pore.
source: This indicates that the VSD does not require the rotation of the C-linker gating ring in order to open the pore, but presumably acts via a membrane-delimited pathway.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as an inference from the cited data.

claim: cAMP alone is not sufficient to open HCN channels.
source: Conversely, cAMP alone is not sufficient to open the channel. In the absence of hyperpolarizing voltages, the channel remains closed even in the presence of high concentrations of cAMP (Gauss et al., 1998; Ludwig et al., 1998; Santoro et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations.

claim: In the absence of hyperpolarizing voltages, HCN channels remain closed even in the presence of high concentrations of cAMP.
source: In the absence of hyperpolarizing voltages, the channel remains closed even in the presence of high concentrations of cAMP (Gauss et al., 1998; Ludwig et al., 1998; Santoro et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations.

claim: In the HCN1 structure obtained at 0 mV, the conformation of the pore is closed even in the presence of cAMP.
source: It is therefore not surprising that in the HCN1 structure, which was obtained at 0 mV, the conformation of the pore is closed even in the presence of cAMP.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction based on the HCN1 structure.

claim: The structure of the gating ring is basically identical in the cAMP-bound (holo) and unbound (apo) HCN1 structures.
source: It is striking, however, that the structure of the gating ring is basically identical in the cAMP-bound (holo) and unbound (apo) HCN1 structures.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction based on the HCN1 structure.

claim: In the presence of cAMP, the gating ring only marginally rotates by about 1 Å and the displacement of S6 is correspondingly minimal.
source: Thus, in the presence of cAMP, the gating ring only marginally rotates by about 1 Å and the displacement of S6 is correspondingly minimal (Lee and MacKinnon, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: The gating ring movement must be under the control of voltage.
source: These functional and structural observations suggest that the gating ring movement must be under the control of voltage, implying the existence of a direct physical contact between the VSD and the C-linker.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as an inference from the structural and functional data.

claim: There is a direct physical contact between the VSD and the C-linker in HCN channels.
source: These functional and structural observations suggest that the gating ring movement must be under the control of voltage, implying the existence of a direct physical contact between the VSD and the C-linker.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as an inference from the structural and functional data.

claim: Hyperpolarizing voltages enhance the affinity of the HCN2 channel for cAMP by up to 3-fold.
source: Thus, Kusch et al. (2010) demonstrated that hyperpolarizing voltages enhance the affinity of the HCN2 channel for cAMP by up to 3-fold.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: The increase in cAMP affinity precedes channel activation in HCN2.
source: In the same study, Kusch et al further showed that the increase in affinity precedes channel activation, underscoring a direct connection between the C-linker/CNBD and VSD, which can occur in either direction, and bypassing the pore.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: There is a direct connection between the C-linker/CNBD and VSD, which can occur in either direction, and bypassing the pore.
source: In the same study, Kusch et al further showed that the increase in affinity precedes channel activation, underscoring a direct connection between the C-linker/CNBD and VSD, which can occur in either direction, and bypassing the pore.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as an inference from the cited data.

claim: The allosteric control of VSD on the affinity of CNBD for cAMP accounts for the difference in affinity measured for the isolated CNBD with respect to those measured in the full length HCN protein.
source: It is worth noting that this allosteric control of VSD on the affinity of CNBD for cAMP most likely accounts for the difference in affinity measured for the isolated CNBD (Lolicato et al., 2011; Saponaro, 2018a; Saponaro et al., 2018b; Saponaro et al., 2014) with respect to those measured in the full length HCN protein (Kusch et al., 2010; Thon et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Binding of cAMP to the CNBD affects the gating charge of the voltage-dependent opening.
source: More recently, the same authors reported that binding of cAMP to the CNBD affects the gating charge of the voltage-dependent opening (Hummert et al., 2018), which provides yet another proof for the model described above.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: A direct physical interaction between the two signal sensing domains, the VSD and the C-linker/CNBD, has not been described so far.
source: Despite the evidence laid out above, a direct physical interaction between the two signal sensing domains, the VSD and the C-linker/CNBD, has not been described so far.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as a knowledge gap.

claim: The HCND appears to contact both the VSD and the C-linker in the HCN1 structure.
source: A close inspection of the HCN1 structure reveals that the HCND appears to contact both the VSD and the C-linker, suggesting the possibility that the VSD and the CNBD may communicate via the HCND without a requirement for the pore as a connecting element.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction based on inspection of the HCN1 structure.

claim: The VSD and the CNBD may communicate via the HCND without a requirement for the pore as a connecting element.
source: A close inspection of the HCN1 structure reveals that the HCND appears to contact both the VSD and the C-linker, suggesting the possibility that the VSD and the CNBD may communicate via the HCND without a requirement for the pore as a connecting element.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as a hypothesis based on structural inspection.

claim: The HCND is critical for the cAMP response in all HCN isoform tested (HCN1, HCN2 and HCN4).
source: We provide evidence that the HCND is indeed critical for the cAMP response in all HCN isoform tested (HCN1, HCN2 and HCN4).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as a finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: The HCND sets the range of voltages at which the channel opens, thus ensuring channel operation at physiological relevant voltages only.
source: In addition, we uncover a second important role of the HCND in gating, which is to set the range of voltages at which the channel opens, thus ensuring channel operation at physiological relevant voltages only.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as a finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: The HCND folds into three short alpha helices HCNa, HCNb and HCNc.
source: It folds into three short alpha helices HCNa, HCNb and HCNc (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: HCNa lies parallel to the plane of the membrane.
source: HCNa lies parallel to the plane of the membrane, HCNb faces the C-linker ring, and HCNc ends in a loop which penetrates the membrane plane and connects the HCND to S1, the first TM helix of the VSD.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the HCN1 structure.

claim: HCNb faces the C-linker ring.
source: HCNa lies parallel to the plane of the membrane, HCNb faces the C-linker ring, and HCNc ends in a loop which penetrates the membrane plane and connects the HCND to S1, the first TM helix of the VSD.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the HCN1 structure.

claim: HCNc ends in a loop which penetrates the membrane plane and connects the HCND to S1.
source: HCNa lies parallel to the plane of the membrane, HCNb faces the C-linker ring, and HCNc ends in a loop which penetrates the membrane plane and connects the HCND to S1, the first TM helix of the VSD.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the HCN1 structure.

claim: The HCND is anchored to the VSD of its own subunit by two hydrophobic residues, F109 and I135, that insert their side chains into two pockets either side of S1.
source: A zoom into the region of interest highlights that the HCND is anchored to the VSD of its own subunit by two hydrophobic residues, F109 and I135, that insert their side chains into two pockets either side of S1 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: R112 and M113 in the HCNb helix form salt bridges with E436 on the B' helix of the adjacent subunit and with K422 on the A' helix of the opposing subunit, respectively.
source: Figure 1C shows two residues in the HCNb helix, R112 and M113, which form salt bridges with E436 on the B' helix of the adjacent subunit (light green) and with K422 on the A' helix of the opposing subunit (dark green), respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Each C-linker is contacted by two different HCNDs and each HCND contacts the C-linkers of two different subunits.
source: Each C-linker is contacted by two different HCNDs and each HCND contacts the C-linkers of two different subunits.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the structural arrangement shown in Figure 1D.

claim: C-linker movements might be directly transmitted to the VSDs and vice-versa.
source: This structural arrangement leads to the prediction that C-linker movements might be directly transmitted to the VSDs and vice-versa.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a prediction based on the structural arrangement.

claim: I177 (I135 in HCN1) is inserted in a hydrophobic pocket formed by the N-terminal and the C-terminal ends of S1 and S2, respectively.
source: The first residue we analyzed is that of I177 (I135 in HCN1) inserted in a hydrophobic pocket formed by the N-terminal and the C-terminal ends of S1 and S2, respectively (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Residues F182 of S1 and L234 of S2 contact the side chain of I177.
source: Specifically, residues F182 of S1 and L234 of S2 contact the side chain of I177, located in the unstructured loop that connects HCNc to S1.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the HCN1 structure.

claim: The interaction of I177 with the VSD is further stabilized by the preceding isoleucine, I176, whose side chain runs parallel to the membrane plane pointing towards a cytosolic loop.
source: The interaction of I177 with the VSD is further stabilized by the preceding isoleucine, I176, whose side chain runs parallel to the membrane plane pointing towards a cytosolic loop (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The cytosolic loop connecting TM S2 to TM S3 of the VSD contains a stretch of hydrophobic residues, I248, I249 and L250 which presumably interact with the I176 side chain.
source: This loop, which connects TM S2 to TM S3 of the VSD, in turn contains a stretch of hydrophobic residues, I248, I249 and L250 which presumably interact with the I176 side chain.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a presumed interaction based on structural inspection.

claim: HCN2 I177D and I177G mutants did not generate detectable HCN-like current.
source: We did not detect any HCN-like current from either of the two mutants (I177D, n = 13; and I177G, n = 18) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: EGFP tagged HCN2 I177D and I177G channels accumulate in intracellular membranes and do not reach the plasma membrane.
source: Confocal microscopy analysis indeed demonstrated that an EGFP tagged version of the respective channels accumulates in intracellular membranes and does not reach the plasma membrane (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: HCN2 I177V and I177A mutants generated currents indistinguishable from the wild type channel in terms of amplitude and gating properties.
source: In contrast, substituting I177 with valine or alanine to gradually reduce the length of the hydrophobic side chain generated currents indistinguishable from the wild type (wt) channel in terms of amplitude and gating properties (Figure 2C,D and Supplementary file 1A), suggesting that a hydrophobic side chain of any length in position 177 is required for proper channel folding and/or trafficking to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: A hydrophobic side chain of any length in position 177 is required for proper channel folding and/or trafficking to the plasma membrane.
source: In contrast, substituting I177 with valine or alanine to gradually reduce the length of the hydrophobic side chain generated currents indistinguishable from the wild type (wt) channel in terms of amplitude and gating properties (Figure 2C,D and Supplementary file 1A), suggesting that a hydrophobic side chain of any length in position 177 is required for proper channel folding and/or trafficking to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the mutagenesis data.

claim: HCN1 I135V/A channels generated a current that was indistinguishable from wt.
source: Similar to HCN2, HCN1 channels carrying the I135V/A mutation (corresponding to I177V/A in HCN2) generated a current that was indistinguishable from wt (I135A current shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 1B; I135V, data not shown),
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: HCN1 I135G mutant generated no detectable current.
source: while the I135G HCN1 mutant generated no detectable current (Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: HCN1 I135G mutant does not reach the plasma membrane.
source: Confocal imaging of HEK293T cells expressing an EGFP tagged HCN1 channel showed that the I135G mutant also does not reach the plasma membrane (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: A hydrophobic side chain in position 135 (HCN1) is crucial for correct folding and/or trafficking of the channel to the plasma membrane.
source: This confirms that a hydrophobic side chain in this position is, also in HCN1, crucial for correct folding and/or trafficking of the channel to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the mutagenesis data.

claim: HCN2 I176D mutation resulted in no current and no channel at the plasma membrane.
source: Mutation into aspartic acid, I176D, resulted in no current and no channel at the plasma membrane (n = 13, Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1A) indicating that this position too does not tolerate a charged residue.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Position 176 in HCN2 does not tolerate a charged residue.
source: Mutation into aspartic acid, I176D, resulted in no current and no channel at the plasma membrane (n = 13, Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1A) indicating that this position too does not tolerate a charged residue.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the mutagenesis data.

claim: HCN2 I176V channel generated a current indistinguishable from wt.
source: When the isoleucine was substituted with a valine (HCN2 I176V), the channel generated a current indistinguishable from wt (Figure 2C,D and Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: HCN2 I176A mutant generated a functional HCN-like current in 28% of cells expressing the mutant.
source: When the length of the side chain was decreased with the I176A mutation, we recorded a functional HCN-like current in 28% of cells expressing HCN2 I176A (n = 10 out of 35 cells tested).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on experimental data.

claim: HCN2 I176A mutant showed a drastic loss of the time-dependent component accompanied by an increase in the instantaneous component of the current.
source: In these cells, we observed a drastic loss of the time-dependent component accompanied by an increase in the instantaneous component of the current (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Application of extracellular cesium (2 mM CsCl) inhibited the HCN2 I176A current almost completely, confirming that the instantaneous component is indeed generated by the mutant channel.
source: Application of extracellular cesium (2 mM CsCl), a known HCN blocker, inhibited the HCN2 I176A current almost completely, confirming that the instantaneous component is indeed generated by the mutant channel (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: HCN2 L250A mutant produced the same phenotype as I176A, including a decrease in the expression levels and a loss of the time dependent component accompanied by an increase of a cesium-sensitive instantaneous component.
source: Interestingly, introducing an alanine mutation in L250, a residue of the S2-S3 loop facing I176, produced the same phenotype of I176A, including a decrease in the expression levels (n = 6 out of 27, or 22% of tested cells exhibited a measurable HCN current) and a loss of the time dependent component accompanied by an increase of a cesium-sensitive instantaneous component (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The findings confirm the interaction of I176 with the S2-S3 loop observed in the HCN1 structure.
source: These findings confirm the interaction of I176 with the S2-S3 loop that we observed in the HCN1 structure.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the mutagenesis data.

claim: HCN1 I134V resulted in wt-like current.
source: Mutation I134V resulted in wt-like current.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on experimental data.

claim: HCN1 I134A resulted in no currents recorded and a lack of channel localization at the plasma membrane.
source: However, unlike I176 in HCN2, residue I134 in HCN1 did not tolerate even the mild substitution I134A. Thus, HCN1 I134A resulted in no currents recorded (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B) and in a lack of channel localization at the plasma membrane (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: A hydrophobic interaction between select residues in the HCN domain and the VSD is essential for proper channel folding, trafficking and function.
source: Taken together these results suggest that a hydrophobic interaction between select residues in the HCN domain and the VSD is essential for proper channel folding, trafficking and function.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the mutagenesis data.

claim: A mild disruption of the interaction between the HCND and the S2-S3 loop, as postulated in the HCN2 I176A and L250A mutants, can result in a significant loss of the voltage-dependent control on channel gating.
source: Even a mild disruption of the interaction between the HCND and the S2-S3 loop, as postulated in the HCN2 I176A and L250A mutants, can result in a significant loss of the voltage-dependent control on channel gating.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the mutagenesis data.

claim: In the HCN1 monomer, the aromatic side chain of F109 is inserted between helices S1 and S4 in a second hydrophobic pocket formed by I284 and M287 in S4, and Y138 in the HCNc-S1 loop.
source: In the HCN1 monomer, the aromatic side chain of this phenylalanine is inserted between helices S1 and S4 in a second hydrophobic pocket formed by I284 and M287 in S4, and Y138 in the HCNc-S1 loop (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A 50 ns long molecular dynamics simulation of HCN1 shows F109 stably inserted in the hydrophobic pocket formed by S1 and S4.
source: A 50 ns long molecular dynamics simulation (MDs) of HCN1 shows F109 stably inserted in this hydrophobic pocket (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: F109E was the only case in which the side chain was found to rotate out of the pocket in molecular dynamics simulations.
source: F109E was the only case in which the side chain was found to rotate out of the pocket (Figure 3B) and interact with the cytosolic solvent.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: F109E was the only case where a distance of less than 2 Å from the water molecules could be measured, indicating that the side chain is hydrated.
source: As a matter of fact, F109E was the only case where a distance of less than 2 Å from the water molecules could be measured, indicating that the side chain is hydrated.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on Solvent Radial Distribution Analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Decreasing the length of the hydrophobic side chain at position 151 in HCN2 progressively shifted the half-activation voltage parameter V1/2 to more depolarized voltages.
source: Decreasing the length of the hydrophobic side chain progressively shifted the half-activation voltage parameter V1/2 to more depolarized voltages (Figure 4A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: HCN2 F151V showed a right shift of 4.4 ± 0.6 mV in V1/2.
source: This right shift was 4.4 ± 0.6 mV for F151V and 13 ± 0.4 mV for F151A.

claim: HCN2 F151A showed a right shift of 13 ± 0.4 mV in V1/2.
source: This right shift was 4.4 ± 0.6 mV for F151V and 13 ± 0.4 mV for F151A.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on experimental data.

claim: HCN2 F151E showed a major shift of 34.7 ± 0.9 mV in V1/2.
source: A major shift of 34.7 ± 0.9 mV was observed for F151E, a mutation that in the MD simulation of HCN1 prevented side chain insertion in the pocket (Figure 3B).

claim: The experimental data are in good agreement with the simulation results, in that a weakening of the hydrophobic interaction is paralleled by a right shift of the voltage activation curve.

claim: Disruption of the hydrophobic pocket at position 151 in HCN2 presumably also affected channel folding and/or trafficking to the plasma membrane, as currents could be measured only in 6 out of 31 cells tested (~19%) for the HCN2 F151E mutant.

evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on experimental data.

claim: HCN2 F151W/M/V/A mutants responded to cAMP like the wt, with a ~ 15 mV positive shift of their V1/2 value.
source: Mutants F151W/M/V/A responded to cAMP like the wt, with a ~ 15 mV positive shift of their V1/2 value (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1A).

claim: The sensitivity of the channel to cAMP is not compromised as long as the hydrophobic interaction at position 151 is maintained to some degree.
source: This suggests that the sensitivity of the channel to cAMP is not compromised as long as the hydrophobic interaction is maintained to some degree.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the mutagenesis data.

claim: The HCN2 F151E mutant is completely insensitive to cAMP.
source: In contrast, the F151E mutant, in which such interaction is fully disrupted, is also completely insensitive to cAMP (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).

claim: The interaction between the HCND and the VSD is required for the allosteric regulation of voltage gating by cAMP.
source: This is consistent with the hypothesis that the interaction between the HCND and the VSD is required for the allosteric regulation of voltage gating by cAMP.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the mutagenesis data.

claim: HCN2 F151D and F151K did not produce measurable currents.
source: In two cases, F151D and F151K, we couldn't measure a current (0/21, 0/26 cells),
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on experimental data.

claim: HCN2 F151R expressed a current indistinguishable from wt in terms of V1/2 and cAMP-response, in 10/24 cells.
source: while F151R expressed a current indistinguishable from wt in terms of V1/2 and cAMP-response, in 10/24 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: Molecular dynamics simulation confirmed that F151D and F151K are exposed to the solvent while F151R is found predominantly in the hydrophobic pocket where it forms an hydrophilic interaction with D183, a residue on S1.
source: Molecular dynamics simulation confirmed that F151D and F151K are exposed to the solvent while F151R is found predominantly in the hydrophobic pocket where it forms an hydrophilic interaction with D183, a residue on S1.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: The interesting behaviour of arginine at position 151 can depend on the hydration properties of its guanidinium moiety that makes dehydration energetically less costly than that of the aliphatic amino group of lysine and to the length of the side chain that can sample conformational space extensively.
source: This interesting behaviour of arginine can depend on the hydration properties of its guanidinium moiety that makes dehydration energetically less costly than that of the aliphatic amino group of lysine and to the length of the side chain that can sample conformational space extensively (Armstrong et al., 2016; Harms et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: HCN1 F109A currents were rarely measurable (6 out of 20 cells, or 30%) indicating poor folding and/or localization of the channel at the plasma membrane.
source: Thus, HCN1 F109A currents were rarely measurable (6 out of 20 cells, or 30%) indicating poor folding and/or localization of the channel at the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on experimental data.

claim: Cells with measurable HCN1 F109A currents displayed an average right shift in the activation curve of 7 mV.
source: Cells with measurable currents displayed an average right shift in the activation curve of 7 mV (Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 1B), matching the phenotype of the equivalent mutant F151A in HCN2.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: HCN1 F109E was not measurable and imaging experiments confirmed that the channel was retained in internal membranes.
source: Mutation HCN1 F109E was not measurable and imaging experiments confirmed that the channel was retained in internal membranes (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Two nearby residues on the HCNb helix, R112 and M113, can form salt bridges with residues K422 on helix A' and E436 on helix B' of the C-linkers of two different subunits.
source: Inspection of the HCN1 structure reveals that two nearby residues on the HCNb helix, R112 and M113, can form salt bridges with residues K422 on helix A' and E436 on helix B' of the C-linkers of two different subunits (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Through the contacts between R112/M113 and K422/E436, the HCND would be directly connected to the C-linker and could, in principle, transmit its movement to the VSD and vice-versa, the movement of the VSD to the C-linker.
source: Through these contacts, the HCND would be directly connected to the C-linker and could, in principle, transmit its movement to the VSD and vice-versa, the movement of the VSD to the C-linker.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a hypothesis based on the structural observations.

claim: A force displacement of the C-linker causes a concerted movement of the C-linker and the HCND; both domains rotate with a similar angle to the z-axis.
source: The computational data show that a force displacement of the C-linker (Figure 5A, position 425), which mimics the conformational changes induced by cAMP binding (Gross et al., 2018), causes a concerted movement of the C-linker and the HCND; both domains rotate with a similar angle to the z-axis (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5B, based on LRT computational data.

claim: The rotational movement of the C-linker and the HCND is transmitted to the VSD, and to the S4 helix in particular, which tilts in response to the movement of the other two domains.
source: The data in Figure 5C show that the rotational movement of the C-linker and the HCND is indeed transmitted to the VSD, and to the S4 helix in particular, which tilts in response to the movement of the other two domains (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5C, based on LRT computational data.

claim: The same rotational movement in the protein can be elicited irrespectively on whether force was applied to the C-linker, the HCND or the S4 helix.
source: The good match observed between data in Figure 5B and D,E confirms that the same rotational movement in the protein can be elicited irrespectively on whether force was applied to the C-linker (Figure 5B), the HCND (Figure 5D) or the S4 helix (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5B,D,E, based on LRT computational data.

claim: The HCND is the transmitting element in a mechanics, which connects the CNBD with the VSD.
source: This underscores that the HCND is the transmitting element in a mechanics, which connects the CNBD with the VSD, and that a disconnection of the HCND from the C-linker should abolish the allosteric effect of cAMP on the voltage dependency of HCN channels.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the LRT computational data.

claim: A disconnection of the HCND from the C-linker should abolish the allosteric effect of cAMP on the voltage dependency of HCN channels.
source: This underscores that the HCND is the transmitting element in a mechanics, which connects the CNBD with the VSD, and that a disconnection of the HCND from the C-linker should abolish the allosteric effect of cAMP on the voltage dependency of HCN channels.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a prediction from the LRT computational data.

claim: HCN2 K464A caused a shift to the right by 9.2 ± 1.3 mV in V1/2.
source: K464A caused a shift to the right by 9.2 ± 1.3 mV, and E478A caused a shift to the left by 18.6 ± 1.4 mV (Figure 6D,E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6D.

claim: HCN2 E478A caused a shift to the left by 18.6 ± 1.4 mV in V1/2.
source: K464A caused a shift to the right by 9.2 ± 1.3 mV, and E478A caused a shift to the left by 18.6 ± 1.4 mV (Figure 6D,E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Combining the K464A and E478A mutations resulted in a V1/2 value similar to the wt.
source: Combining the two mutations resulted in a V1/2 value similar to the wt (100.6 ± 0.9 mV and 96.7 ± 1.2 mV for K464A-E478A and wt, respectively; not statistically different) (Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The two single mutations K464A and E478A responded to cAMP with a normal shift in the activation curve.
source: Interestingly, when we tested the effect of cAMP (15 µM) we found that the two single mutations responded to cAMP with a normal shift in the activation curve (K464A = +15.7 ± 0.9 mV; E478A = +13.5 ± 0.9 mV; wt = +16.7 ± 1.9 mV) accompanied by an increase in maximal current and an acceleration of the activation kinetics similar to that observed in the wt.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on experimental data.

claim: The HCN2 K464A-E478A double mutant was no longer able to respond to cAMP.
source: However, as predicted by our hypothesis, the double mutant was no longer able to respond to cAMP (+2.3 ± 1 mV, not statistically different from control), either at the 15 μM concentration or at a higher concentration of 100 μM (Figure 6C–F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The addition of cAMP is still able to affect channel deactivation in the K464A-E478A mutant, strongly suggesting that cAMP is bound to the CNBD in the mutant and that the disruption of the HCND/C-linker interaction results in a loss of the coupling between ligand binding and channel activation.
source: The observation that the addition of cAMP is still able to affect channel deactivation in the K464A-E478A mutant, however, strongly suggests that cAMP is bound to the CNBD in the mutant and that the disruption of the HCND/C-linker interaction indeed results in a loss of the coupling between ligand binding and channel activation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The effects measured on the deactivation pathway are independent from the effects of the same mutations on the activation pathway.
source: Our observation that the effects measured on the deactivation pathway are independent from the effects of the same mutations on the activation pathway confirms earlier functional and modeling studies by other groups (Altomare et al., 2001; Hummert et al., 2018; Männikkö et al., 2005; Wicks et al., 2011) which indicated that opening and closing in HCN channels occur through different pathways, and that these respective pathways are differentially affected by cAMP binding.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: Opening and closing in HCN channels occur through different pathways, and these respective pathways are differentially affected by cAMP binding.
source: Our observation that the effects measured on the deactivation pathway are independent from the effects of the same mutations on the activation pathway confirms earlier functional and modeling studies by other groups (Altomare et al., 2001; Hummert et al., 2018; Männikkö et al., 2005; Wicks et al., 2011) which indicated that opening and closing in HCN channels occur through different pathways, and that these respective pathways are differentially affected by cAMP binding.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: E478 and R154 interact in HCN2.
source: Since the perturbation energies are unequal, we can conclude that the two positions are not independent (coupled) and that E478 and R154 interact.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on mutant cycle analysis.

claim: The interaction energy between E478 and R154 is – 2.0 kcal/mol.
source: The interaction energy between the two sites, assessed by the non-additivity factor ΔΔG (see Materials and methods) is – 2.0 kcal/mol.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on mutant cycle analysis.

claim: The C-linker interacts with the HCND at two sites, E478 and K464.
source: From all the above, we conclude that the C-linker interacts with the HCND at two sites, E478 and K464.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the mutagenesis data.

claim: Disrupting the interaction between the C-linker and the HCND, as in the double mutant K464A- E478A, prevents cAMP effect in HCN2.
source: Disrupting their interaction, as in the double mutant K464A- E478A, prevents cAMP effect in HCN2.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the mutagenesis data.

claim: In HCN4, the double mutant K543A-E557A showed no shift in the V1/2 in response to 30 µM cAMP, compared to the normal ~20 mV right shift in the wt.
source: In HCN4, the double mutant K543A-E557A showed no shift in the V1/2 in response to 30 µM cAMP, compared to the normal ~20 mV right shift in the wt.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on experimental data.

claim: In HCN4, cAMP was still able to cause a significant change in the time constant of deactivation in the K543A-E557A mutant, implying effective binding to the CNBD.
source: Similar to HCN2, however, cAMP was still able to cause a significant change in the time constant of deactivation implying effective binding to the CNBD (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: HCN1 currents measured in the whole cell configuration already have an activation curve fully shifted to the right due to the higher affinity of HCN1 for cAMP and endogenous levels of cAMP present in HEK293T cells.
source: Because the higher affinity of HCN1 for cAMP, compared to the other HCN isoforms, allows this channel to respond to endogenous levels of cAMP present in HEK293T cells, HCN1 currents measured in the whole cell configuration already have an activation curve fully shifted to the right (Saponaro et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: The R549E mutation in human HCN1 reduces the affinity for cAMP by about 1000 times.
source: This can be demonstrated using a mutation in the CNBD, R549E in human HCN1, which reduces the affinity for cAMP by about 1000 times (Chen et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: The R549E mutation induces a leftward shift in V1/2 of ~9 mV, which is the maximal ΔV1/2 response of HCN1 to cAMP binding.
source: As shown in Figure 7A, the R549E mutation induces a leftward shift in V1/2 of ~9 mV, which is the maximal ΔV1/2 response of HCN1 to cAMP binding.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The HCN1 K422A-E436A double mutant and R549E mutant showed a similar V1/2.
source: The two channels showed a similar V1/2 (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The double mutation K422A-E436A in HCN1 prevents the transmission of the signal exerted by endogenous levels of cAMP.
source: This suggests that the double mutation that disconnects the C-linker from the HCND prevents the transmission of the signal exerted in HCN1 by endogenous levels of cAMP.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Addition of 15 µM cAMP did not affect either HCN1 K422A-E436A or R549E channels.
source: As expected, addition of 15 µM cAMP did not affect either channels (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, and Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Disconnecting the C-linker from the HCND results in loss of the cAMP effects on channel activation in HCN1, HCN2, and HCN4.
source: We found that, in these isoforms too, disconnecting the C-linker from the HCND resulted in loss of the cAMP effects on channel activation similar to HCN2 (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: The mechanism by which the HCND transmits the cAMP signal from the C-linker to the VSD is conserved in all three isoforms which show a response to cyclic nucleotides, namely HCN1, HCN2 and HCN4.
source: Collectively, these data are consistent with the prediction of the LRT analysis that the HCND transmits the cAMP signal from the C-linker to the VSD and that such a mechanism is conserved in all three isoforms which show a response to cyclic nucleotides, namely HCN1, HCN2 and HCN4.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: The HCND ensures the correct folding and trafficking of the channel to the plasma membrane.
source: Our data show that HCND ensures the correct folding and trafficking of the channel to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: The HCND represents the structural element that allows the integration of the two different signals, voltage and cAMP, which are critical for channel gating.
source: Importantly, the data also indicate that HCND represents the structural element that allows the integration of the two different signals, voltage and cAMP, which are critical for channel gating.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: Anchoring of the HCND to the VSD is essential for correct folding and trafficking of the channel to the plasma membrane.
source: Anchoring of the HCND to the VSD is essential for correct folding and trafficking of the channel to the plasma membrane, as demonstrated by mutant channels HCN1 I135G and HCN1 F109E which are both retained in the secretory pathway (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: HCN2 channels lacking the N terminus do not reach the plasma membrane.
source: Our findings confirm and extend previous reports showing that HCN2 channels lacking the N terminus do not reach the plasma membrane, a phenotype attributed to the critical role of the N terminus in channel assembly (Proenza et al., 2002; Tran et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: The HCNb helix contains a conserved ER export motif (106VNKFSL111) wherein L111 provides the key signal.
source: Prior studies had further suggested that the HCNb helix contains a conserved ER export motif (106VNKFSL111) wherein L111 provides the key signal (Pan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: The HCND is the structural element that functionally couples the VSD with the C-linker/CNBD.
source: Our study uncovered a major contribution of the HCND to channel function, by providing evidence that the HCND is the structural element that functionally couples the VSD with the C-linker/CNBD.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: By forming a mechanical continuum between the voltage sensing and ligand binding elements, the HCND is able to mutually transmit conformational information directly between the CNBD and the VSD, bypassing the pore.
source: By forming a mechanical continuum between the voltage sensing and ligand binding elements, the HCND is able to mutually transmit conformational information directly between the CNBD and the VSD, bypassing the pore.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: Contact between the HCND and the voltage sensor is mediated by hydrophobic interactions, wherein an aromatic side chain (F109/F151 in HCN1 and HCN2 respectively) inserts into a hydrophobic pocket formed by S1 and S4 residues.
source: Contact between the HCND and the voltage sensor is mediated by hydrophobic interactions, wherein an aromatic side chain (F109/F151 in HCN1 and HCN2 respectively) inserts into a hydrophobic pocket formed by S1 and S4 residues.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: Contact between the HCND and the C-linker is established by means of salt bridges in a hydrophilic environment.
source: In contrast, contact between the HCND and the C-linker is established by means of salt bridges in a hydrophilic environment.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: The HCND/C-linker contacts show an interesting bifurcated interaction pattern where two adjacent amino acids on the HCND form a common point of interaction from which they branch to form salt bridges with the A'-helix and B'-helix of C-linkers from the adjacent and opposite subunits, respectively.
source: The HCND/C-linker contacts show an interesting bifurcated interaction pattern. Two adjacent amino acids on the HCND form a common point of interaction from which they branch to form salt bridges with the A'-helix and B'-helix of C-linkers from the adjacent and opposite subunits, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: Binding of cAMP generates an iris-like movement in the 'gating ring' portion of the C-linker, which is formed by the A' and B' helices.
source: Previous experimental and computational studies have indicated that binding of cAMP generates an iris-like movement in the 'gating ring' portion of the C-linker, which is formed by the A' and B' helices (Craven and Zagotta, 2004; Gross et al., 2018; Lee and MacKinnon, 2017; Marchesi et al., 2018; Shin et al., 2004; Weißgraeber et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: The planar rotational movement of the C-linker is translated into an upward rotational movement of the HCND due to the nature of the attachment between the C-linker helices and HCND.
source: Due to the nature of the attachment between the C-linker helices and HCND, this planar rotational movement is translated into an upward rotational movement of the HCND.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: The upward rotational movement of the HCND results into a tilting of the S4 domain due to the tight hydrophobic interactions formed between the HCND and the VSD.
source: This, in turn, results into a tilting of the S4 domain (Video 1) due to the tight hydrophobic interactions formed between the HCND and the VSD.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: The mechanical link between the VSD, HCND, and C-linker is conserved between the different HCN isoforms.
source: Our experimental data also show that such mechanical link is conserved between the different HCN isoforms, thus providing a general mechanism for the modulation by voltage and cAMP, a feature common to the HCN1, HCN2 and HCN4 isoforms.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: Destabilizing the interaction between the HCND and the loop connecting S2 with S3 of the VSD (mutants HCN2 I176A and HCN2 L250A) led to a distinct decrease in the time-dependent component of the HCN current, accompanied by a corresponding increase in the instantaneous component.
source: For one, destabilizing the interaction between the HCND and the loop connecting S2 with S3 of the VSD (mutants HCN2 I176A and HCN2 L250A) led to a distinct decrease in the time-dependent component of the HCN current, accompanied by a corresponding increase in the instantaneous component.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: The loss in the voltage dependence of opening and closing in HCN2 I176A and L250A mutants results in a 'leaky' channel.
source: This indicates a loss in the voltage dependence of opening and closing, resulting in a 'leaky' channel.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: The strong shift in the voltage dependence of the F151E mutation towards more depolarized potentials (+ 34 mV) implies that the HCND normally keeps the VSD in a position, which is unfavorable for channel opening.
source: The strong shift in the voltage dependence of the F151E mutation towards more depolarized potentials (+ 34 mV) implies that the HCND normally keeps the VSD in a position, which is unfavorable for channel opening.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: The HCND acting via F151 exerts an inhibitory action on the VSD, reminiscent of the previously highlighted inhibitory effect of CNBD on the channel.
source: In other words, the HCND acting via F151 exerts an inhibitory action on the VSD, reminiscent of the previously highlighted inhibitory effect of CNBD on the channel (Wainger et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: In less severe mutants (e.g. F151V/A), in which the hydrophobic contact is maintained but weakened, the V1/2 values are progressively right shifted, which is in good agreement with a model in which a reduced impact of HCND on the VSD lowers the energy barrier for channel opening.
source: Such a model is also supported by the behavior of less severe mutants (e.g. F151V/A), in which the hydrophobic contact is maintained but weakened. In these mutants, the V1/2 values are progressively right shifted. This is in good agreement with a model in which a reduced impact of HCND on the VSD lowers the energy barrier for channel opening.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: The conformational change in the C-linker, which is generated by the binding of cAMP, is transmitted via the HCND to the VSD, lowering the energy barrier for channel opening.
source: Both computational and experimental data suggest that the conformational change in the C-linker, which is generated by the binding of cAMP, is transmitted via the HCND to the VSD, lowering the energy barrier for channel opening.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: As long as the HCND is connected to the hydrophobic pocket formed by S4, cAMP is still able to shift the voltage dependence of the channel to more positive voltages as in mutants HCN2 F151V and F151A.
source: As long as the HCND is connected to the hydrophobic pocket formed by S4, cAMP is still able to shift the voltage dependence of the channel to more positive voltages as in mutants HCN2 F151V and F151A.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: cAMP has no longer an impact on the voltage dependence of the channel once the contact between the VSD and the HCND is completely disrupted as in mutant HCN2 F151E.
source: In contrast, cAMP has no longer an impact on the voltage dependence of the channel once the contact between the VSD and the HCND is completely disrupted as in mutant HCN2 F151E.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: The contact between the HCND and the C-linker is equally essential for the allosteric regulation of gating.
source: Just like the contact between VSD and the HCND is important for the allosteric regulation of gating, the contact between the HCND and the C-linker is equally essential.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: Mutants which disrupt the contacts between the C-linker and the HCND modulate the gating behavior of the channels.
source: In line with the idea of a mechanic continuum between the three elements, we find that mutants, which disrupt the contacts between the C-linker and the HCND, modulate the gating behavior of the channels.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: Disruption of the contacts between the C-linker and the HCND eliminated the effect of cAMP on channel activation (e.g. HCN2 K464A-E478A or HCN4 K543-E557).
source: Disruption of these contacts eliminated the effect of cAMP on channel activation (e.g. HCN2 K464A-E478A or HCN4 K543-E557).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: The HCND serves as a coupling and transmission element between CNBD and VSD.
source: This is in good agreement with the model in which the HCND serves as a coupling and transmission element between CNBD and VSD.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: Isoform-specific responses to cAMP emerge from the mechanisms that connect the cytosolic to the TM domains.
source: The mutational analysis conducted in parallel in HCN1 and HCN2 (and HCN4) gave more consistent results in the case of C-linker/HCND interaction than of HCND/VSD highlighting that isoform-specific responses to cAMP emerge from the mechanisms that connect the cytosolic to the TM domains.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: Removal of the inhibition exerted by the voltage sensor on the ability of the cAMP signal to open the pore requires both voltage and the physical connection of the VSD to the C-linker mediated by the HCND.
source: Our data now show that removal of this inhibition requires both voltage and the physical connection of the VSD to the C-linker mediated by the HCND.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: The rotational movement of the C-linker following binding of cAMP to the CNBD translates via the HCND into a small movement of the VSD that may preactivate the channel by lowering the voltage required to move the sensor.
source: In this scenario, the rotational movement of the C-linker following binding of cAMP to the CNBD translates via the HCND into a small movement of the VSD that may preactivate the channel by lowering the voltage required to move the sensor (Kusch et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: The autoinhibitory effect of the CNBD, which constrains gating to more hyperpolarized potentials, is directly mediated by the HCND.
source: Thus, we suggest that the autoinhibitory effect of the CNBD, which constrains gating to more hyperpolarized potentials (Wainger et al., 2001), is directly mediated by the HCND.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: The HCND might prevent or promote the extent of the movement of the VSD depending on the bound or unbound state of the CNBD.
source: The latter might then prevent or promote the extent of the movement of the VSD depending on the bound or unbound state of the CNBD.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: Ligand binding to the CNBD promotes movement of the voltage sensor in a concentration dependent manner, including when the channel is not preactivated by voltage.
